source: 3,180 bands that played multiple shows from 2013-2016
why: This is a count of the records in the dataset (a description of the data's size), not a finding. web_data.csv has 3,180 band rows.

source: What three years and 75,000 shows in New York tell us about the chance your favorite band will succeed.
why: This is a description of the dataset's size, not a finding, and the 75,000 figure is not in the files: web_data.csv has 37,086 band-show rows (29,422 unique date-venue pairs).

source: Sylvan Esso was one of over 7,000 bands to play a small show in the NYC area that year.
why: The count of all bands that played a small show in 2013 (over 7,000) is not in the files; web_data.csv contains only the 3,180 bands that played another show from 2014 to 2016.

source: of the 7,000 bands that headlined a small venue (less than 700 capacity) in the NYC area in 2013, less than half even played another show from 2014 to October of 2016.
why: The denominator (all ~7,000 bands that headlined a small venue in 2013) is not in the files. web_data.csv contains only the 3,180 bands that did play again, so the share that played again cannot be computed.

source: But only 21 out of the 7,000 bands reached Sylvan Esso’s level of “making it”: headlining a show of over 3,000 capacity.
why: The 7,000-band denominator is not in the files. The raw tier-2 count in web_data.csv is 22, not 21; the extra band is Torres, who is absent from web_made.csv. The story's 21-band roster (web_made.csv) is reproduced in the twenty-one-made-bands fact; the 21-out-of-7,000 ratio itself cannot be computed because the 7,000-band denominator is not in the files.

source: The Brooklyn based band played 24 small to medium sized shows in New York from 2009 to 2014, before headlining Terminal Five in December 2014.
why: web_data.csv's Lucius history starts on 2012-02-18 and contains 22 shows (16 before the 2014-12-06 Terminal 5 show), not 24 shows from 2009 to 2014. The pre-2012 shows are absent from the file.

source: 5.3 years from their first small show in NYC until they made it big
why: The chart's Lucius path starts at Barbès (60) on Aug 16, 2009, but web_data.csv's first Lucius show is 2012-02-18; the data therefore gives about 2.8 years to the 2014-12-06 Terminal 5 show, not 5.3 years.

source: 4.6 years; 3.6 years; 3.5 years; 3.3 years; 3.0 years; 2.9 years; 2.5 years; 2.4 years; 2.3 years; 2.2 years; 1.8 years; 1.5 years; 1.4 years; 1.3 years; 1.2 years; 1.0 years
why: These chart labels give each made band's time from its first NYC small show to its big show. web_data.csv's show histories begin in 2012, so earlier shows are missing for bands with a longer history; the per-band durations computed from the files do not reproduce the chart's full set of labels.

source: The band rose faster than any other US based band in our dataset
why: The 'less than two years' duration is reproduced in the sylvan-esso-under-two-years fact, but the 'faster than any other US based band' ranking cannot be computed: the files contain no band nationality or country field.

source: The bands that make it from outside the U.S. are more likely to have short journeys to “making it”.
why: The files contain no band nationality or country field, so journeys to making it cannot be compared between U.S. and non-U.S. bands.

source: The following list shows some of the 21 bands who made it, and when and where they hit it big.
why: The 21-band membership is reproduced in the twenty-one-made-bands fact, but the list's dates and venues are not all reproducible from the data: the data's first big-tier headlining show matches 9 of the 10 dated entries, while Mayer Hawthorne's data shows an earlier Madison Square Garden show on 2016-02-19 before his 2016-06-24 Terminal 5 show. The data also codes some support slots as headlining shows.

source: For every Chance the Rapper there are thousands of rappers that never play a show with more than a couple hundred people.
why: This is a rhetorical comparison, not a computed finding, and the files have no full universe of rappers or genre data.

source: For every Lake Street Dive, there are hundreds of promising bands that break up because they lost on their members.
why: This is a rhetorical comparison, not a computed finding, and the files have no band-breakup or member-change data.
